chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ubayd Allah ibn Ahmad, both together, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Zayd al-Narsi, from Ali ibn Farqad, the companion of al-Sabiri, who said:

A man bequeathed his estate to me and ordered me to perform Hajj with it on his behalf. So I looked into it and found it to be a small amount, not sufficient for Hajj. So I asked Abu Hanifa and the jurists of the people of Kufa, and they said: 'Give it in charity on his behalf.'

So when I performed Hajj, I met Abdullah ibn al-Hasan during the Tawaf. So I asked him and said to him: 'Indeed, a man from your mawali (clients/followers) from the people of Kufa died and bequeathed his estate to me and ordered me to perform Hajj with it on his behalf. So I looked into it, but it was not sufficient for Hajj. So I asked the jurists from our side, and they said:
He said to me: 'This is Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the Hujr, so go to him and ask him.'

He said: So I entered the Hujr, and there was Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) beneath the Mizab (spout of the Kaaba), facing with his face towards the House, supplicating. Then he turned towards me and saw me, so he said: 'What is your need?'
I said: 'May I be sacrificed for you! I am a man from the people of Kufa, from your mawali.' He said: 'Leave that aside, what is your need?'

I said: 'A man died and bequeathed his estate that I should perform Hajj with it on his behalf. So I looked into it, but it was not sufficient for Hajj. So I asked the jurists who are with us, and they said:
He said: 'What did you do?' I said: 'I gave it in charity.'

He said: 'You are responsible (guaranteed), except if it happens that it is not sufficient to perform Hajj with it from Makkah. So if it is not sufficient to perform Hajj with it from Makkah, then there is no responsibility upon you. And if it is sufficient to perform Hajj with it from Makkah, then you are responsible.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a bequest for Hajj is insufficient for the ritual?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential divergence between the Kufan jurists, who prioritized the general principle of fulfilling the bequest through charity when funds were insufficient, and Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who introduced a nuanced condition of actual sufficiency for liability. The Imam’s ruling establishes that the executor’s guarantee (daman) is contingent upon the bequested amount being capable of performing Hajj; if it falls short, charity suffices without penalty, reflecting a precise application of equity in Shia fiqh. This distinction underscores the Shia emphasis on contextual assessment over rigid formalism in executing wills.
